section.title: Absolute convergence and stronger tests
section.p: Alternating series taught us that cancellation can make a divergent positive series turn into a convergent signed series.
But cancellation is fragile. It depends on order and balance.
A stronger kind of convergence ignores cancellation entirely. It asks whether the total size of all terms is finite:
If that positive series converges, then the original signed series converges no matter how the signs behave.

exercise.title: What is the difference between absolute and conditional convergence?

statement.p: Absolute convergence means \sum |a_k| converges. Conditional convergence means the signed series converges while the absolute series diverges. In your own words, why does finite total size force ordinary convergence, and why is cancellation a weaker, more fragile reason to converge?

hint.p: If the total size is finite, the positive and negative parts are each finite, so their difference is finite. Conditional convergence keeps an infinite supply of both signs and balances them by order.

exercise.title: Why does the Ratio Test compare a series with a geometric series?

statement.p: The Ratio Test looks at \lim |a_{k+1}/a_k|. In your own words, why does a limit strictly less than 1 make the terms eventually shrink like a geometric series, and why is the test especially natural for factorials and exponentials?

hint.p: If consecutive terms are eventually no larger than a fixed fraction r<1 of the previous term, comparison with \sum r^k takes over. Factorials and exponentials change by a clean multiplicative factor from one term to the next.

exercise.title: When is the Root Test the natural test?

statement.p: The Root Test looks at \lim \sqrt[k]{|a_k|}. In your own words, why does a k-th power in the term invite a k-th root, and why is a limit strictly less than 1 again a geometric comparison?

hint.p: Taking the k-th root undoes a k-th power. If the roots settle below 1, then eventually |a_k|\le r^k for some r<1.
